definition: Ascertain means to find something out for certain — to pin a fact down through deliberate checking or inquiry.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word ascertain. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know ascertain should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Before quoting a price, the movers ascertained exactly how many stairs stood between the truck and the fourth-floor door.
Estimate is weaker than ascertain: an estimate gets you usefully close to the number, while ascertaining means checking until the fact is pinned down exactly.
Establish goes further than ascertain — once you ascertain a fact you are sure of it yourself, but establishing it fixes the fact publicly, beyond dispute for everyone else too.
To determine is to settle a question — fix the answer so it stands. Ascertain overlaps, but it points at the digging: a fact already out there, hidden, that you go and find out for certain.

To discover is to come upon something new, often by chance. Ascertain is deliberate — you set out after the fact, check, and make sure of it. An old coin can be discovered by accident; its age is ascertained on purpose.
to take something as true without checking
to offer an answer with nothing to back it
She delivered the committee's verdict with a certitude her own notes did not entirely support.
Ascertain means to find something out for certain — to pin a fact down through deliberate checking or inquiry.

The supply convoy could not roll until the engineers had ascertained whether the river ice would bear loaded trucks, so they spent a full day drilling test holes every hundred meters and measuring each one to the centimeter — all that work to come away owning a single number.
Ascertain fits because the engineers set out after one hidden fact and checked until they were sure of it.
That deliberateness is the word's signature: you discover a thing by stumbling on it, but you ascertain it on purpose.
And where this unit's surmise builds a likely guess out of clues, ascertaining ends with the guesswork gone.
Ascertain is the careful, slightly starchy verb of reports and procedures — investigators ascertain the cause, clerks ascertain eligibility.
Use it when the finding-out is deliberate and the answer must be exact; in casual prose, find out is the natural choice.
Its neighbors in this unit sit on either side of it: surmise stops at a well-grounded guess, and scrutinize names the looking rather than the learning.

When our stadium claimed a record crowd, a local blog said the number was padded, and the argument ran for a week.
The club could have shrugged.
Instead it hired an auditor to ascertain the true count.
She did not guess and she did not average.
She pulled the turnstile logs, matched them against ticket scans, and counted the staff gate by hand.
The number she published was four hundred lower than the announcement and two thousand higher than the blog's guess.
Nobody loved her figure, but nobody argued with it either.
It was not an opinion; it was the count, checked until it was certain.
